def: Information we collect, like numbers or answers. Everyone's height in your class is data.
Puts things into groups, like eye color or yes/no. You count it; you don't average it.
A number you can do math with, like height or a test score.
All the values and how often each one shows up. It tells you the shape, center and spread.
A bar graph for numbers. Each bar shows how many values land in a range, like 60 to 70 inches.
A picture made from five numbers: smallest, Q1, median, Q3 and biggest. The box holds the middle half of the data.
The average. Add up all the numbers, then divide by how many there are.
The middle number after you line them up from smallest to biggest.
Biggest minus smallest. A quick look at how spread out the data is.
They cut the data into four equal parts. Q1 is the 25% mark and Q3 is the 75% mark.
Q3 minus Q1: how wide the middle half of the data is.
About how far the values usually are from the mean. Small means bunched up; big means spread out.
A value far away from the rest. A common rule: more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3.
Lopsided. Skew is named after the long tail: a tail stretching right means skewed right.
Both sides look about the same, like a mirror image.
Not pushed around much by outliers. The median is resistant; the mean is not.
How many standard deviations a value is from the mean. z = 2 means "two steps above average."
The percent of values at or below a number. The 90th percentile beats about 90% of the group.
The smooth, symmetric bell curve. Lots of things in nature come close to it.
In a normal curve, about 68% of values are within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SDs and 99.7% within 3.
A graph of dots that shows how two number variables go together, like hours studied and test score.
A number from −1 to 1 for how strong a straight-line pattern is, and which way it goes.
The best straight line through a scatterplot. It makes the squared misses as small as possible.
How much the line goes up or down for each 1 step to the right.
The predicted y when x is 0. Sometimes it doesn't make sense in real life.
Actual minus predicted: how far a dot sits above or below the line.
The percent of the change in y that the line explains using x.
Using the line to predict far outside the data you have. Risky!
Everyone or everything you want to learn about.
The smaller group you actually look at.
Every group of that size has the same chance of being picked, like drawing names from a hat.
When the way you collect data keeps pushing your answer the wrong way.
Split everyone into similar groups first (like grades 9 to 12), then randomly pick from each group.
Split into groups that each look like a mini-population (like classrooms), randomly pick a few whole groups, and use everyone in them.
You watch and record without changing anything. It can't prove cause and effect.
You do something to the subjects (a treatment) to see what happens.
What you do to the subjects in an experiment, like a new study app.
The group that gets nothing new, or a placebo, so you have something to compare against.
A fake treatment, like a sugar pill, so people can't tell which group they're in.
Keeping people from knowing who got which treatment, so it can't change their answers.
A hidden variable linked to both things you're studying, which makes it hard to tell what caused what.
Using chance, like a coin flip, to decide who gets which treatment. It keeps the groups fair.
How likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (always).
One happening doesn't change the chance of the other, like two coin flips.
Can't happen at the same time, like rolling a 2 and a 5 on one die.
The chance of something when you already know something else happened. Written P(A | B).
A number that comes from a chance process, like the number of heads in 3 flips.
The long-run average if you repeated the chance process many, many times.
Counting successes in a set number of tries, where each try is yes/no with the same chance.
Counting how many tries it takes to get the first success.
The more times you repeat something, the closer your results get to the true chance.
A number about the whole population, usually unknown. P for Population.
A number from your sample. S for Sample.
What you'd see if you took lots and lots of samples and graphed the statistic from each one.
When samples are big enough (n ≥ 30 is the usual rule), sample means make a bell shape, even if the population doesn't.
How much a statistic usually wobbles from sample to sample.
A statistic whose sampling distribution is centered right on the true value.
A range of believable values for the true answer, like "between 52% and 60%."
How often the method catches the true value in the long run, like 95% of the time.
The ± part of a confidence interval. Bigger samples make it smaller.
H₀, the null, says "nothing special is going on." Hₐ, the alternative, is what you're looking for evidence of.
If H₀ were true, the chance of getting results at least as extreme as yours just by luck. Small p-value: hard to blame luck.
Your cutoff for "small," often 0.05. If the p-value is below α, you reject H₀.
Rejecting H₀ when it was actually true. A false alarm.
Not rejecting H₀ when it was actually false. A missed alarm.
The chance your test catches a real effect when there is one.
How many standard errors your result is from what H₀ predicts, like a z or a t.
Checks before you trust a test: Random data, sample under 10% of the population, and a big enough sample (Normal or Large counts).
A bell curve with fatter tails, used for means when you don't know σ. Its shape depends on the degrees of freedom.
A number that sets the exact shape of a t or chi-square curve. For one mean, df = n − 1.
Two numbers from the same person or matched pair, like before and after. Subtract to get one list of differences.
Adds up (observed − expected)² ÷ expected. A big χ² means the counts don't fit what you expected.
The counts you'd get if H₀ were exactly true. Each one should be at least 5.
